title: Lesson 12 - A2.1.6 Physical Threats
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How can physical security protect devices, data and restricted areas?

sections.heading: What is physical security?
sections.text: Physical security means protecting devices, data, people and buildings from physical threats, such as theft, damage or unauthorised access.
points: Example: a company leaves several laptops in an unlocked office overnight. A thief gets in and steals laptops holding customer information and company files
Application: a school keeps student records on laptops in a staff-only room, protected by a locked door, security pass and CCTV
Those measures make it harder for unauthorised people to get in and steal devices containing sensitive data

sections.heading: Device theft
sections.text: Devices can contain sensitive or confidential data, which makes them a target for theft.
points: Laptops, tablets and smartphones can be stolen from workplaces or while travelling
USB drives and other storage devices can be lost or stolen
If a device is stolen, criminals may be able to access or extract the data on it
Standard protections (from Lessons 1 and 6): encrypt devices and USB drives, never leave devices unattended, lock storage away

sections.heading: Physical areas
sections.text: Poor security in buildings or restricted areas can let unauthorised people in. They could steal or damage equipment such as servers and computers, or get at sensitive data on servers or databases.
points: Example: a server room is left unlocked, so any employee can walk in
Risk: someone could damage equipment, steal hardware or access sensitive data
Protection: locks, security passes, CCTV and regular access reviews
Only people with a business need should be allowed access, and access should be reviewed and audited regularly

sections.heading: Security reviews: suggested timescales
sections.text: Security reviews check that only authorised people have access to restricted areas and systems.

head: When
What to check
rows: Daily
Doors, alarms and restricted areas are secure
Monthly
Review access logs, security passes and CCTV
Every 6 months
Check staff access and remove unnecessary permissions
Annually
Carry out a full physical security audit
After an incident
Review security immediately and make improvements

sections.heading: Managing access
points: Least privilege: users should only have access to what they need
Automated tools: use software to manage and record access rights where possible
Manager approval: privileged access should need approval
Remove access: revoke access immediately when staff leave or change roles
Keep records: document and log reviews for auditing and accountability
The goal: the right people have the right access, and unnecessary access is removed

sections.heading: User vulnerability
sections.text: People can create security risks through mistakes, poor security practices or weak processes.

head: Type
Example
rows: Accidental data leaks
Sending sensitive information to the wrong person, or posting private information publicly
Sharing passwords
Sending passwords by email, or saying them where others can hear
Weak security processes
Poor password-reset procedures, or hidden 'backdoors' attackers could exploit

points: Example: an employee emails a confidential document to the wrong person, with the password in the same email
Risk: an unauthorised person can open the sensitive information
Prevention: check recipients carefully, and never share passwords through insecure methods

sections.heading: Worked scenario: risks and measures
sections.text: The slides' scenario: a company stores sensitive customer data on laptops, USB drives and servers. Here's one way to answer 'identify the risks and suggest a measure for each' (my worked answer, so try it yourself first):

head: Weakness
Risk
Measure
rows: Laptops left unattended
Stolen, and customer data accessed
Never leave unattended; lock away; encrypt laptops
USB drives not stored securely
Lost or stolen, exposing data
Encrypt them and keep them in a locked cabinet
Server room often unlocked
Equipment damaged or stolen; data accessed
Locks, security passes and CCTV
Too many people can enter the server room
More chances for damage, theft or misuse
Least privilege: only those with a business need
Passwords shared by email
An unauthorised person gets the password and logs in
Never share passwords by email; training; a password policy
Access rights not reviewed
Leavers or role-changers keep access they shouldn't have
Regular reviews (every 6 months) and remove access when staff leave

keyIdea: Devices and storage hold sensitive data, so theft, unlocked rooms and careless people all put data at risk. Physical security (locks, passes, CCTV), least-privilege access, regular reviews and good habits keep the wrong people away from devices and data.

quiz.q: Which types of equipment might contain sensitive data?
o: Laptops, smartphones, USB drives and servers
quiz.e: Any device or storage media can hold sensitive or confidential data.

quiz.q: Which is an example of something that could be physically stolen from an organisation?
quiz.e: Laptops, phones, tablets, USB drives and even server hardware can be stolen.

quiz.q: What could an organisation use to stop unauthorised people entering a restricted area?
o: A locked door with security passes
quiz.e: Locks, security passes and CCTV restrict and monitor access.

o: Protecting devices, data, people and buildings from theft, damage or unauthorised access
quiz.e: It covers physical threats, not just digital ones.

quiz.q: Why is the theft of a USB drive a security risk?
o: Whoever has it may be able to access the sensitive data on it
quiz.e: Small storage devices are easily lost or stolen, and the data goes with them (unless encrypted).

quiz.q: A server room is often left unlocked. What risk does this create?
o: Equipment could be damaged or stolen, and data accessed
quiz.e: Anyone can walk in and steal, damage or access servers.

quiz.q: Who should have access to a restricted area such as a server room?
o: Only people with a business need
quiz.e: Least privilege: only those who need it for their job.

quiz.q: How often should a full physical security audit be carried out?
quiz.e: Annually: a full audit. Daily, monthly and 6-monthly checks fill in between.

quiz.q: How often should access logs, security passes and CCTV be reviewed?
quiz.e: Monthly review of logs, passes and CCTV.

quiz.q: When should an employee's access be removed if they leave the company?
quiz.e: Revoke access immediately when staff leave or change roles.

quiz.q: An employee emails a confidential document to the wrong person, with the password in the same email. What's the risk?
o: The email will be too big
The wrong person can open the sensitive information
quiz.e: Sending the password with the file defeats the protection.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a weak security process?
quiz.e: Weak processes, like easy password resets or hidden backdoors, can be exploited.

quiz.q: What should happen after a security incident?
o: Review security immediately and make improvements
quiz.e: Review straight away to fix whatever allowed the incident.

o: Users only have access to what they need
quiz.e: No more access than the job needs.

quiz.q: Which TWO are physical security measures?
quiz.e: Also: security passes, security staff, locked cabinets, alarms.

quiz.q: Why should access reviews be documented and logged?
quiz.e: Records show who had access and what was checked.

apply.title: Risk and fix
apply.intro: Pick the risk, or the best measure, for each situation. This is exactly what the slides' scenario task asks.

items.task: A sales rep leaves their laptop on a train seat while getting a coffee.
o: Device theft: never leave devices unattended; encrypt them
items.e: Unattended devices can be stolen, and the data with them.

items.task: USB drives with customer data are kept in an open tray on reception.
o: They could be stolen: encrypt them and lock them away
They will run out of storage
items.e: Store removable media securely and encrypt it.

items.task: The server room door is propped open because it gets too hot inside.
o: Unauthorised access to servers: keep it locked (and fix the cooling)
items.e: Any unauthorised person could damage, steal or access the servers.

items.task: Forty staff have passes to the server room, but only three ever need to go in.
o: Too much access: apply least privilege
items.e: Only people with a business need should have access.

items.task: A manager emails a staff member: 'The admin password is Summer2024!'
items.e: Never share passwords by email or where others can hear.

items.task: An employee left six months ago, but their security pass still opens the office doors.
o: Access not revoked: remove access immediately when staff leave
items.e: Revoke access immediately and review access regularly.

o: Doors, alarms and restricted areas are secure
items.e: Daily: doors, alarms and restricted areas. Annual: the full audit.

items.task: Which check should happen EVERY 6 MONTHS?
o: Check staff access and remove unnecessary permissions
items.e: Every 6 months: staff access and unnecessary permissions.

items.task: A staff member reads out their password on a busy open-plan office phone call.
o: Sharing passwords where others can hear
items.e: Saying passwords aloud is a user vulnerability.

items.task: Anyone can reset a staff password just by phoning the helpdesk and giving a name.
items.e: Poor password-reset procedures can be exploited by attackers.

items.task: After a break-in, a company waits until its next annual audit to change anything. What should it do instead?
o: Review security immediately and make improvements
items.e: Review straight away after an incident.

items.task: A school wants to protect a staff room where laptops with student records are kept. Which combination is best?
o: A locked door, security passes and CCTV

pts: Protecting devices, data, people and buildings
from physical threats such as theft, damage or unauthorised access

exam.q: 2. Explain why the theft of a USB drive is a security risk.
pts: USB drives can store sensitive or confidential data and are small, so they're easily lost or stolen
so whoever has the drive may be able to access or extract that data (especially if it isn't encrypted)
exam.tip: Point + linked consequence. Mentioning encryption shows extra understanding.

exam.q: 3. A server room is often left unlocked. Explain the security risk this creates.
pts: Unauthorised people could enter the server room
and damage equipment, steal hardware or access the sensitive data stored on the servers
exam.tip: Who can get in + what they could do.

exam.q: 4. Give two physical security measures an organisation could use.
pts: Any one: locks / locked doors
A second, different one: security passes / CCTV / security staff / locked storage

exam.q: 5. Explain what is meant by least privilege and why it improves security.
pts: Users should only have access to what they need for their job
so fewer people can reach restricted areas or data, reducing the chance of theft, damage or misuse

exam.q: 6. Describe a suitable schedule of security reviews for an organisation.
pts: Daily: check doors, alarms and restricted areas are secure
Monthly: review access logs, security passes and CCTV
Every 6 months: check staff access and remove unnecessary permissions
Annually: a full physical security audit (and immediately after any incident)
exam.tip: Learn the slides' timescales. One mark per correctly matched time and check.

exam.q: 7. Explain two ways people can create security risks for an organisation.
pts: Way 1, e.g. accidental data leaks: sending sensitive information to the wrong person
so an unauthorised person could read confidential data
Way 2, e.g. sharing passwords by email or saying them aloud / weak processes like poor password resets
so attackers could get the password, or exploit the process, and access systems
exam.tip: Use the slides' three user vulnerabilities: accidental leaks, sharing passwords, weak processes.

exam.sc: A company stores sensitive customer data on laptops, USB drives and servers. It has several weaknesses: laptops are sometimes left unattended; USB drives are not stored securely; the server room is often left unlocked; too many employees have access to the server room; employees sometimes share passwords by email; and access rights are not regularly reviewed.
exam.q: 8. Identify four security risks in this company and suggest a suitable security measure for each.
pts: Risk 1, e.g. unattended laptops could be stolen and customer data accessed
Measure 1, e.g. never leave laptops unattended, lock them away and encrypt them
Risk 2, e.g. USB drives not stored securely could be lost or stolen
Measure 2, e.g. encrypt USB drives and keep them in a locked cabinet
Risk 3, e.g. the unlocked server room lets anyone damage, steal or access servers
Measure 3, e.g. locks, security passes and CCTV; least privilege for the many staff who have access
Risk 4, e.g. passwords shared by email could be read by the wrong person / access rights not reviewed
Measure 4, e.g. never email passwords and use a password policy / review access every 6 months and remove leavers immediately
exam.tip: This is the slides' scenario task. 1 mark per risk + 1 per matching measure. Each measure must fix ITS risk.
